screens.title: Defining and Calling Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Functions let you group steps into a named, reusable unit that you can invoke whenever you need the same behavior. In Python you declare a function with the keyword def, give it a name and parameters, and then write the indented body that performs the task. Functions simplify programs by removing repetition, isolating behavior for testing, and making code easier to read. You will learn not only the syntax to define and call functions but also practical aspects like how arguments map to parameters, why return matters, how docstrings help others (and tools) understand your code, and common mistakes beginners make. For example, a simple greeting function shows how a parameter becomes a placeholder for actual data when you call the function. Later we will practice converting temperatures using two small functions and learn how mutable objects can change outside a function when modified in place. By the end of this chapter you should be able to write clear functions, call them correctly with positional or keyword arguments, and document them with useful docstrings. Consider how you would package a repeated calculation in your own programs — that idea is the practical heart of functions.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Defining and Calling Functions
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Defining and Calling Functions

Learn why functions reduce repetition, how parameters and arguments work, and how to return values and document behavior with docstrings.

In this lesson you'll see concrete examples and a hands-on temperature conversion activity.
You will practice positional and keyword arguments and learn common errors to avoid.
Why this matters

Functions let you package logic once and reuse it safely. They make testing, debugging, and collaboration easier because each function has a clear responsibility and inputs.

Explore Key Topics
def keyword
Syntax for defining functions
Parameters & Arguments
Placeholders and provided values
Return & Side Effects
Return values vs mutable changes
Visual Concept
Recipe → Function
Ingredients

Parameters act like recipe ingredients. They are placeholders that receive values when the function is called.

Example: name, length, width
Steps

The function body executes steps using the parameters and may return a result to the caller.

Example: calculate area, format greeting
Execution flow
Call the function name with parentheses; Python runs the block and returns control when finished. If a value is returned, the caller can use it immediately.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will define and explain the role of functions in Python, write functions with parameters and return values, and choose between positional and keyword arguments when calling them. You will also write clear docstrings so other developers and tools can understand your functions, and identify the common errors that happen during definition and invocation. For example, you will practice creating a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit and its inverse, including docstrings that describe inputs and returned values. You will spot mistakes like forgetting parentheses when calling a function or providing too many arguments and see why Python raises a TypeError. Together these objectives build practical skills: breaking programs into modular pieces, communicating intent through docstrings, and avoiding common pitfalls that lead to subtle bugs. These skills improve code readability, reduce duplication, and make debugging faster. As you work, try to name parameters descriptively and run small tests to confirm the return values you expect.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to writing functions, you'll perform targeted practice to internalize correct calling patterns and avoid pitfalls. This includes implementing a temperature converter pair, running small tests to confirm returned values, and seeing how mutable objects can be modified inside a function. Practicing with controlled examples makes it easier to spot errors like missing parentheses, mismatched argument counts, or multiple values for the same parameter. Each objective pairs a practical task with a safety check: write the function, test expected outputs, read or write a docstring, then watch for TypeError messages when arguments do not match. This pattern trains you to think both about the shape of data a function expects and the effect your function has when it runs. Short tests and clear parameter names reduce debugging time and make your functions safer to reuse in larger programs. Consider writing a tiny test after every new function you define to confirm it returns the expected result.

screens.title: What is a function?
screens.narratorSegment: A function is a named block of reusable code designed to perform a specific task. Defining a function packages a sequence of steps under a single identifier so you can run those steps by calling the function name later. This promotes modularity and reduces repetition in your programs. For example, a greeting function that prints or returns a personalized message captures the steps needed to format and present the text. The definition uses the keyword def followed by a valid identifier, parentheses, and a colon. The indented block that follows is the function body and will not run until the function is called. One common misconception is that defining a function runs its code; it does not. A definition only creates the function object. Calling the function, which requires parentheses even when there are no parameters, executes the body. Another misconception is thinking functions must return values; a function that prints values is allowed, but if you expect to use a result later you must return it explicitly. Example: a greet_person function can accept a parameter called name and then print a greeting. Key takeaway: functions organize behavior, avoid repetition, and separate definition from execution — ask yourself which repeated operations in your code belong inside a function.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is a function?
Definition

A function is a named block of code that runs when called. It accepts parameters and may return a value. Definitions do not execute the body.

Example
def greet_person(name):
  """Prints a personalized greeting message."""
  print(f"Hello, {name}!")

# Call the function:
greet_person("Alice")
Takeaway: Definition creates, call executes. Use parentheses to call a function.
Misconception: Defining a function runs code immediately — it does not.
Why functions help
  • Reduce repetition by centralizing logic you call multiple times.
  • Improve readability by naming a block according to its purpose.
  • Enable testing and reuse across programs.
Check your understanding
If you define a function but forget parentheses when trying to run it, you will reference the function object instead of executing it. How would you spot this in a program? Look for no output and values that are function objects instead of expected results.

screens.title: def syntax and indentation
screens.narratorSegment: Writing a correct function definition requires three simple pieces: the def keyword, a valid function name, and parentheses that may contain parameters, followed by a colon. After that, the function body must be indented. Python uses indentation to group the body, so consistent indentation is essential; mixing tabs and spaces or misaligned blocks will raise an IndentationError. Use descriptive names that follow Python identifier rules: start with a letter or underscore and avoid spaces or special characters. In practice, a compact example looks like a small procedure: def calculate_area(length, width): return length * width. You can write the return on the same line for a single expression, but most code uses multiple lines with an explicit return to keep docstrings and comments readable. A common beginner error is forgetting the colon after the header or writing the body at the same indentation level as def. Another subtle issue is shadowing built-in names; avoid names like list or str for your functions. Example code below demonstrates a properly formatted function with a docstring, parameters, and a return. Review your editor's visible whitespace mode to prevent indentation bugs and remember: the colon marks the start of the indented function body.

keyIdea.title: Syntax rules
keyIdea.text: Use def name(params): then an indented body. Keep indentation consistent and avoid reusing built-in names.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › def syntax and indentation
Code example
def calculate_area(length, width):
  """Calculates the area of a rectangle.

  Args:
    length (int or float): length of the rectangle.
    width (int or float): width of the rectangle.

  Returns:
    int or float: area of the rectangle.
  """
  return length * width

area1 = calculate_area(10, 5)
print(f"Area 1: {area1}")
Note: keep consistent indentation. The docstring appears directly after the header and before other code.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the colon at the end of the header raises a SyntaxError.
  • Incorrect indentation raises IndentationError; enable visible whitespace in your editor.
  • Using built-in names for functions can shadow core behavior and cause confusion.
Pro tip: Keep docstrings and returns clear so your function's contract is obvious when reused.

screens.title: Calling a function
screens.narratorSegment: Calling a function transfers program control to the function's body, executes its steps, and then returns control to the caller. The syntax requires the function name followed by parentheses. Parentheses are essential: without them you reference the function object rather than executing it. Execution flow looks like this: the caller evaluates any argument expressions, creates parameter bindings inside the function, runs the body, evaluates a return expression if present, and sends that value back. A common beginner oversight is expecting side effects or return values without understanding this flow. For example, if a function only prints a message, calling it will display the message but assigning its call to a variable will set that variable to None unless the function returns a value. To practice, call functions with literal constants, expressions, or other function calls as arguments. When mixing positional and keyword arguments, positional ones must appear first. A brief process checklist: evaluate arguments, bind parameters, run body, return value or None, resume caller. Keep this order in mind when debugging unexpected results or TypeError messages because argument evaluation happens before the function body starts running.

keyIdea.text: A call evaluates arguments, binds parameters, runs the function, and returns a value or None; parentheses invoke execution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Calling a function
Step-by-step
1. Evaluate argument expressions and prepare values.
2. Bind those values to the function's parameter names.
3. Execute the indented body in the function's scope.
4. Evaluate a return expression if present and send the result back; otherwise return None.
Concrete example
def greet_user():
  print("Hello, Cohortia learner!")

# Calling the function runs its body and prints:
greet_user()

# Without parentheses you get the function object:
obj = greet_user
print(obj)  # shows function object, not execution
Misconception: Assigning a call to a variable is the same as assigning the function — they are different. One executes, the other references.

screens.title: Parameters vs Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Parameters and arguments are often used interchangeably in casual speech, but they have distinct roles. A parameter is a named variable in the function definition that acts as a placeholder for the data the function will operate on. An argument is the actual value you pass when calling the function. For instance, in a definition def greet_person(name): name is a parameter; when you call greet_person("Alice"), the string Alice is the argument. This distinction matters when reading documentation, writing tests, or diagnosing mismatches between what a function expects and what it receives. Another practical distinction: parameters are part of a function's contract and are visible in the function signature and docstring; arguments are runtime values and can be expressions like 2 + 3 or calls to other functions. A common confusion arises when mixing up order and naming: positional arguments map by position to parameters, while keyword arguments map by name and can improve readability. Finally, remember parameter names live inside the function scope and do not affect variables outside unless a mutable object is modified in place. As a quick check, name parameters descriptively and craft test calls that exercise both positional and keyword usage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Parameters vs Arguments
Parameter (definition)
A named variable in the function header that defines what inputs the function expects. Example: def power(base, exponent): base and exponent are parameters.
Docstring tip
List parameter types and purpose so callers know what to pass and what the function returns.
Argument (call site)
The actual value provided when calling the function. It can be a literal, variable, expression, or keyword argument like exponent=3.
Example calls
power(2, 3)            # positional
power(base=2, exponent=3)  # keyword
power(2, exponent=3)     # mix: positional first, then keywords
Common confusion

Passing the same value both positionally and as a keyword causes a TypeError for multiple values for the same parameter. Keep positional arguments first to avoid errors when mixing styles.

screens.title: Positional vs Keyword Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Positional arguments are matched to parameters by order. They are concise and common for short functions with few parameters. Keyword arguments explicitly name the parameter and set its value, which improves readability when functions have many parameters or when you want to skip arguments with defaults. A key rule in Python is that positional arguments must come before keyword arguments in a call. Mixing them out of order or providing a positional after a keyword will raise an error. Keyword arguments are especially useful when functions accept many optional parameters; you can name only the ones you need. A practical example: calculate_area(10, 5) uses positional mapping to length and width, while calculate_area(width=5, length=10) uses keywords so order doesn't matter. A common misconception is that keyword arguments are slower or inferior — they are primarily a readability tool and commonly used in APIs. Use keywords when clarity matters, and use positionals when the order is natural and short. When debugging argument errors, read the error message: Python will state missing required positional arguments or unexpected keyword arguments to guide you toward a fix.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Positional vs Keyword Arguments
Positional
Match by order. Good for short, conventional parameter lists. Example: calculate_area(10, 5).
Pros: concise. Cons: less explicit for many parameters.
Keyword
Match by name. Great for clarity and optional parameters. Example: calculate_area(width=5, length=10).
Pros: readable, order-independent. Cons: longer to type.
Rule

When mixing both styles in one call, write all positional arguments first, then keyword arguments to avoid TypeError.

screens.title: Return values and None
screens.narratorSegment: The return statement sends a value from a function back to its caller. If a function reaches the end without hitting an explicit return, Python returns None implicitly. Relying on printed output instead of return will not provide a value to the caller, which can lead to unexpected None values in expressions or assignments. For example, if calculate_area printed the result instead of returning it, assigning area1 = calculate_area(10, 5) would set area1 to None and break later calculations. Use return when the caller must use the result. Another common pattern is returning multiple values as a tuple to provide structured results. A misconception is that print and return are interchangeable; they are not. Print communicates to the console, return communicates to the program. When testing, always assert the returned value rather than inspecting printed output. If a function is intended only for side effects, it may omit return, but document that behavior in the docstring so callers know not to expect a value. Closing question: when would you choose to return a value versus relying on a side effect such as printing or modifying a global variable?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Return values and None
Example: return
def calculate_area(length, width):
  return length * width

area = calculate_area(10, 5)
print(area)  # 50
Key takeaway: return provides a usable value to the caller.
Example: print only
def show_area(length, width):
  print(length * width)

result = show_area(10, 5)
print(result)  # None
Misconception: printing is not returning. Use return when other code must use the value.

screens.title: Docstrings and documenting functions
screens.narratorSegment: Docstrings are string literals placed immediately after the def header and serve as the primary in-code documentation for a function. Triple-quoted docstrings can span multiple lines and typically describe what the function does, list parameters and their types, explain return values, and note side effects or exceptions. Tools and IDEs often display docstrings as quick help, and you can access them at runtime through the function's doc attribute. Writing good docstrings makes your code self-documenting and helps teammates and future you use the function correctly. For example, include a short summary line, followed by an Args section that names parameters and expected types, and a Returns section describing what is returned. A common mistake is writing comments inside the body instead of a docstring; docstrings are specifically picked up by documentation tools. When you write a function for the temperature conversion activity, include docstrings that say which units the input and output use so tests and readers know what to expect. Finally, keep docstrings concise yet informative — they are not a place for implementation detail but for an A P I contract.

keyIdea.text: Place a triple-quoted string right after def to explain purpose, parameters, returns, and side effects for users and tools.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Docstrings and documenting functions
Good docstring pattern
def power(base, exponent):
  """
  Calculates the power of a base number to a given exponent.

  Args:
    base (int or float): The base number.
    exponent (int): The exponent.

  Returns:
    int or float: The result of base raised to the power of exponent.
  """
  return base ** exponent
Why docstrings matter
  • They appear in help tools and IDEs via __doc__.
  • They document the expected types and behavior for callers and future maintainers.
  • They clarify whether a function returns a value or only performs side effects.
Tip: Keep summary line short, then add details in sections for Args and Returns.

screens.title: Mutable arguments and side effects
screens.narratorSegment: Mutable objects such as lists or dictionaries can be modified in place by functions, producing side effects that are visible outside the function. This differs from returning a new value. For example, when a function accepts a list and calls append on it, the original list passed by the caller is changed because both the caller and the function reference the same object. A typical demonstration from the chapter shows a function that appends to a list and prints it inside the function. After the call, the outside list includes the appended element, and assigning the result of the function to a variable yields None if the function had no return statement. Beginners often expect the function to leave the original object untouched or to return a modified copy; when this is not the case, bugs arise. To avoid unintended side effects, either return a new object or clearly document that the function mutates its input. When debugging, inspect the object before and after the call and prefer immutable types when you want safety. Final takeaway: know whether your function is intended to mutate inputs or return new values, and document that in the docstring.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Mutable arguments and side effects
Example: modifying a list
def modify_list(my_list):
  my_list.append(4)
  print(f"Inside function: {my_list}")

data = [1, 2, 3]
result = modify_list(data)
print(f"Outside function (data): {data}")
print(f"Outside function (result): {result}")
This prints that the list was changed inside the function and that the function returned None because it had no explicit return.
Guidelines
  • Document mutation in the docstring so callers know the function changes the input.
  • Prefer returning a new object when you need immutability guarantees.
  • Use immutable types when possible to avoid accidental shared-state bugs.

screens.title: Common errors and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When working with functions, several recurring errors appear. A TypeError commonly occurs when you supply the wrong number of arguments or use the same parameter twice with both positional and keyword forms. For example, calculate_discount(price=100, 10) will raise an error because a positional argument comes after a keyword. Another common mistake is forgetting parentheses when calling a function, which leaves you with a function object rather than executing it. SyntaxError and IndentationError arise from malformed def headers or inconsistent indentation. To debug these issues, read the traceback carefully: Python points to the call causing the problem and usually names the missing or unexpected parameter. Reproduce the issue with a small test call and simplify arguments until the function runs. For side effects, inspect mutable objects before and after calls to determine whether the function modified them in place. Use docstrings and small tests to confirm expected behavior. A useful assessment question from the chapter asks which mixed call is correct; practicing these scenarios builds intuition about argument order and naming. Final takeaway: systematic small tests and reading error messages will quickly guide you to the fix.

Error examples
TypeError from wrong argument order or count; IndentationError from incorrect indentation; forgetting parentheses yields a function object instead of execution.

fullNarratorScript:
Functions let you group steps into a named, reusable unit that you can invoke whenever you need the same behavior. In Python you declare a function with the keyword def, give it a name and parameters, and then write the indented body that performs the task. Functions simplify programs by removing repetition, isolating behavior for testing, and making code easier to read. You will learn not only the syntax to define and call functions but also practical aspects like how arguments map to parameters, why return matters, how docstrings help others (and tools) understand your code, and common mistakes beginners make. For example, a simple greeting function shows how a parameter becomes a placeholder for actual data when you call the function. Later we will practice converting temperatures using two small functions and learn how mutable objects can change outside a function when modified in place. By the end of this chapter you should be able to write clear functions, call them correctly with positional or keyword arguments, and document them with useful docstrings. Consider how you would package a repeated calculation in your own programs — that idea is the practical heart of functions.

By the end of this chapter you will define and explain the role of functions in Python, write functions with parameters and return values, and choose between positional and keyword arguments when calling them. You will also write clear docstrings so other developers and tools can understand your functions, and identify the common errors that happen during definition and invocation. For example, you will practice creating a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit and its inverse, including docstrings that describe inputs and returned values. You will spot mistakes like forgetting parentheses when calling a function or providing too many arguments and see why Python raises a TypeError. Together these objectives build practical skills: breaking programs into modular pieces, communicating intent through docstrings, and avoiding common pitfalls that lead to subtle bugs. These skills improve code readability, reduce duplication, and make debugging faster. As you work, try to name parameters descriptively and run small tests to confirm the return values you expect.

In addition to writing functions, you'll perform targeted practice to internalize correct calling patterns and avoid pitfalls. This includes implementing a temperature converter pair, running small tests to confirm returned values, and seeing how mutable objects can be modified inside a function. Practicing with controlled examples makes it easier to spot errors like missing parentheses, mismatched argument counts, or multiple values for the same parameter. Each objective pairs a practical task with a safety check: write the function, test expected outputs, read or write a docstring, then watch for TypeError messages when arguments do not match. This pattern trains you to think both about the shape of data a function expects and the effect your function has when it runs. Short tests and clear parameter names reduce debugging time and make your functions safer to reuse in larger programs. Consider writing a tiny test after every new function you define to confirm it returns the expected result.

A function is a named block of reusable code designed to perform a specific task. Defining a function packages a sequence of steps under a single identifier so you can run those steps by calling the function name later. This promotes modularity and reduces repetition in your programs. For example, a greeting function that prints or returns a personalized message captures the steps needed to format and present the text. The definition uses the keyword def followed by a valid identifier, parentheses, and a colon. The indented block that follows is the function body and will not run until the function is called. One common misconception is that defining a function runs its code; it does not. A definition only creates the function object. Calling the function, which requires parentheses even when there are no parameters, executes the body. Another misconception is thinking functions must return values; a function that prints values is allowed, but if you expect to use a result later you must return it explicitly. Example: a greet_person function can accept a parameter called name and then print a greeting. Key takeaway: functions organize behavior, avoid repetition, and separate definition from execution — ask yourself which repeated operations in your code belong inside a function.

Writing a correct function definition requires three simple pieces: the def keyword, a valid function name, and parentheses that may contain parameters, followed by a colon. After that, the function body must be indented. Python uses indentation to group the body, so consistent indentation is essential; mixing tabs and spaces or misaligned blocks will raise an IndentationError. Use descriptive names that follow Python identifier rules: start with a letter or underscore and avoid spaces or special characters. In practice, a compact example looks like a small procedure: def calculate_area(length, width): return length * width. You can write the return on the same line for a single expression, but most code uses multiple lines with an explicit return to keep docstrings and comments readable. A common beginner error is forgetting the colon after the header or writing the body at the same indentation level as def. Another subtle issue is shadowing built-in names; avoid names like list or str for your functions. Example code below demonstrates a properly formatted function with a docstring, parameters, and a return. Review your editor's visible whitespace mode to prevent indentation bugs and remember: the colon marks the start of the indented function body.

Calling a function transfers program control to the function's body, executes its steps, and then returns control to the caller. The syntax requires the function name followed by parentheses. Parentheses are essential: without them you reference the function object rather than executing it. Execution flow looks like this: the caller evaluates any argument expressions, creates parameter bindings inside the function, runs the body, evaluates a return expression if present, and sends that value back. A common beginner oversight is expecting side effects or return values without understanding this flow. For example, if a function only prints a message, calling it will display the message but assigning its call to a variable will set that variable to None unless the function returns a value. To practice, call functions with literal constants, expressions, or other function calls as arguments. When mixing positional and keyword arguments, positional ones must appear first. A brief process checklist: evaluate arguments, bind parameters, run body, return value or None, resume caller. Keep this order in mind when debugging unexpected results or TypeError messages because argument evaluation happens before the function body starts running.

Parameters and arguments are often used interchangeably in casual speech, but they have distinct roles. A parameter is a named variable in the function definition that acts as a placeholder for the data the function will operate on. An argument is the actual value you pass when calling the function. For instance, in a definition def greet_person(name): name is a parameter; when you call greet_person("Alice"), the string Alice is the argument. This distinction matters when reading documentation, writing tests, or diagnosing mismatches between what a function expects and what it receives. Another practical distinction: parameters are part of a function's contract and are visible in the function signature and docstring; arguments are runtime values and can be expressions like 2 + 3 or calls to other functions. A common confusion arises when mixing up order and naming: positional arguments map by position to parameters, while keyword arguments map by name and can improve readability. Finally, remember parameter names live inside the function scope and do not affect variables outside unless a mutable object is modified in place. As a quick check, name parameters descriptively and craft test calls that exercise both positional and keyword usage.

Positional arguments are matched to parameters by order. They are concise and common for short functions with few parameters. Keyword arguments explicitly name the parameter and set its value, which improves readability when functions have many parameters or when you want to skip arguments with defaults. A key rule in Python is that positional arguments must come before keyword arguments in a call. Mixing them out of order or providing a positional after a keyword will raise an error. Keyword arguments are especially useful when functions accept many optional parameters; you can name only the ones you need. A practical example: calculate_area(10, 5) uses positional mapping to length and width, while calculate_area(width=5, length=10) uses keywords so order doesn't matter. A common misconception is that keyword arguments are slower or inferior — they are primarily a readability tool and commonly used in APIs. Use keywords when clarity matters, and use positionals when the order is natural and short. When debugging argument errors, read the error message: Python will state missing required positional arguments or unexpected keyword arguments to guide you toward a fix.

The return statement sends a value from a function back to its caller. If a function reaches the end without hitting an explicit return, Python returns None implicitly. Relying on printed output instead of return will not provide a value to the caller, which can lead to unexpected None values in expressions or assignments. For example, if calculate_area printed the result instead of returning it, assigning area1 = calculate_area(10, 5) would set area1 to None and break later calculations. Use return when the caller must use the result. Another common pattern is returning multiple values as a tuple to provide structured results. A misconception is that print and return are interchangeable; they are not. Print communicates to the console, return communicates to the program. When testing, always assert the returned value rather than inspecting printed output. If a function is intended only for side effects, it may omit return, but document that behavior in the docstring so callers know not to expect a value. Closing question: when would you choose to return a value versus relying on a side effect such as printing or modifying a global variable?

Docstrings are string literals placed immediately after the def header and serve as the primary in-code documentation for a function. Triple-quoted docstrings can span multiple lines and typically describe what the function does, list parameters and their types, explain return values, and note side effects or exceptions. Tools and IDEs often display docstrings as quick help, and you can access them at runtime through the function's doc attribute. Writing good docstrings makes your code self-documenting and helps teammates and future you use the function correctly. For example, include a short summary line, followed by an Args section that names parameters and expected types, and a Returns section describing what is returned. A common mistake is writing comments inside the body instead of a docstring; docstrings are specifically picked up by documentation tools. When you write a function for the temperature conversion activity, include docstrings that say which units the input and output use so tests and readers know what to expect. Finally, keep docstrings concise yet informative — they are not a place for implementation detail but for an A P I contract.

Mutable objects such as lists or dictionaries can be modified in place by functions, producing side effects that are visible outside the function. This differs from returning a new value. For example, when a function accepts a list and calls append on it, the original list passed by the caller is changed because both the caller and the function reference the same object. A typical demonstration from the chapter shows a function that appends to a list and prints it inside the function. After the call, the outside list includes the appended element, and assigning the result of the function to a variable yields None if the function had no return statement. Beginners often expect the function to leave the original object untouched or to return a modified copy; when this is not the case, bugs arise. To avoid unintended side effects, either return a new object or clearly document that the function mutates its input. When debugging, inspect the object before and after the call and prefer immutable types when you want safety. Final takeaway: know whether your function is intended to mutate inputs or return new values, and document that in the docstring.
